say.text: Night shift. A 9-month-old with known TOF turned deeply blue after a distressing blood draw. Your junior wrote this plan on the handover sheet, and one step is wrong.
1) Knee-chest position. 2) Oxygen. 3) IV furosemide. 4) IV fluid bolus. Which step do you strike out?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask of each step: does it help a blue child with a hypercyanotic spell, or does it treat a different problem, like a failing heart?
Tempting: squatting looks like comfort, not treatment. But it is the first-line physical step: **knee-chest positioning** increases systemic vascular resistance.
So step 1 stays. Look again at which step treats a different problem.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is worth a second look: a step that needs no drug is still a treatment. It raises systemic vascular resistance.

say.text: Tempting: fluid in a struggling child sounds like it would overload the heart. But in a spell, **IV fluid boluses** improve RV filling.
So step 4 stays. Which step treats congestion that this child does not have?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so notice the reflex: this is a spell, not heart failure. Fluids are on the list because they improve RV filling.

say.text: Yes, strike out the furosemide. A blue, distressed child looks like heart failure, but spells need a rapid and aggressive approach, and a diuretic is not one of the steps.
The real steps: knee-chest (raises systemic vascular resistance), oxygen (pulmonary vasodilation), IV fluid boluses (improve RV filling).
Page two of the same handover lists the reason for each drug. One reason is backwards.
Oxygen: pulmonary vasodilation. Beta-blocker: decreases heart rate and aids RV filling. Phenylephrine: lowers systemic afterload. Which line is wrong?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Recall the logic of knee-chest position. Which direction should systemic resistance move in a spell, and does that line point the same way?
Tempting: the lungs are not the obstruction, so oxygen may seem pointless. But **oxygen** is given to cause pulmonary vasodilation, and that line is correct.
Check the drug whose stated reason would push resistance the wrong way.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so re-read it: oxygen's job is pulmonary vasodilation, exactly as the note says.

say.text: Tempting: slowing the heart in a sick child feels dangerous. But **IV beta-blockers** decrease heart rate and aid RV filling further, so that line is right.
Look for the drug whose reason contradicts knee-chest.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so re-read it: the note's beta-blocker reason matches the source.

say.text: Yes. **IV phenylephrine** increases systemic afterload; it does not lower it. Knee-chest also raises systemic vascular resistance.
Every correct step pushes the same way: systemic resistance up, or RV filling better. Lowering resistance would be the reversed logic.
The spell settles. Your junior summarises the surgical plan for the parents, and one line is wrong.

1) The timing of complete repair is still debated; StatPearls describes deferring it until after 3 months of age. 2) A Blalock-Taussig shunt joins the subclavian artery to the ipsilateral branch pulmonary artery. 3) A pulmonary valve can only be replaced by open surgery. Which line is wrong?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: One line uses the word "only". Check whether the source allows a second route.
Tempting: a textbook should give one age. But **the timing of TOF repair is still in debate**, and StatPearls describes deferring complete repair to after the first 3 months of life.
So line 1 is fine. Find the line that closes a door the source leaves open.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note it: this is a debated topic, and the line says so honestly.

say.text: Tempting: a shunt sounds like it should join two big vessels. But the **Blalock-Taussig shunt** connects the subclavian artery to the ipsilateral branch pulmonary artery, so line 2 is accurate.
Look for the line that closes a door the source leaves open.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so re-read it: subclavian artery to ipsilateral branch pulmonary artery is exactly the source's description.

say.text: Yes. "Only" is the planted error: pulmonary valve replacement can be achieved surgically or by a transcatheter approach.
Lines 1 and 2 were right: repair timing is debated, and the Blalock-Taussig shunt joins the subclavian artery to the ipsilateral branch pulmonary artery.

choices.label: Go deeper: who gets a shunt first?

say.text: Your junior adds: "Every neonate with TOF gets a shunt first, then repair later." Is that right?

choices.label: Right, all neonates are palliated first
Wrong, staging is for high-risk features only
Wrong, no infant is ever palliated first

say.text: Tempting: the first surgical treatment of TOF was a palliative shunt. But one group does not palliate patients who present as neonates without high-risk features.

Tempting: palliation sounds outdated. But the same authors reserve staging with initial palliation for infants with high-risk features: low birth weight or prematurity, and small or discontinuous pulmonary arteries.
Yes. Initial palliation is reserved for high-risk features: low birth weight or prematurity, and small or discontinuous pulmonary arteries.
Drawbacks include the limited lifespan of the shunt and an increased incidence of late sudden death. Morbidities include pulmonary artery stenosis and distortion.
Years later the child is in the follow-up clinic after complete repair. A peer's clinic summary says: "Commonest reason to reoperate after repair is a residual VSD."
What do you do with this line?

choices.label: Keep it, the original lesion recurs
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about what the surgeon had to reconstruct to relieve the obstruction, and what that does to the valve afterwards.
Tempting: you expect the original defect to come back. But the repair itself causes the trouble: **pulmonary regurgitation** results from reconstruction of the RVOT.
And **pulmonary insufficiency** is the most common indication for reoperation.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth keeping: the commonest reoperation indication is pulmonary insufficiency, not a recurrence of the original lesions.

say.text: Tempting: arrhythmias are a genuine late problem. Arrhythmias can occur after repair, including **ventricular tachycardia**.
But the most common indication for reoperation is pulmonary insufficiency.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the two: ventricular tachycardia is a real late problem, but pulmonary insufficiency is the commonest reoperation indication.

say.text: Yes. **Pulmonary regurgitation** results from reconstruction of the RVOT, and pulmonary insufficiency is the most common indication for reoperation.
The clinic summary also says: "Repaired children are safe from rhythm problems." Which correction is accurate?

choices.label: Rhythm problems occur only before repair
VT occurs; 40-50% of adults have ventricular arrhythmias
Arrhythmias are common but sudden death never follows repair
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: The correction must cover both arrhythmias and late sudden death. Which option keeps both?
Tempting: repair fixes the anatomy, so rhythm problems seem solved. But arrhythmias can occur after TOF repair, including **ventricular tachycardia**.
Tempting: the first half is right, since 40-50% of adults with repaired TOF can have ventricular arrhythmias.
But sudden death does follow: the risk is 6-9% 30 years after the surgical procedure.
Yes. Ventricular tachycardia can occur, 40-50% of adults with repaired TOF can have ventricular arrhythmias, and the risk of sudden death is 6-9% 30 years after the surgical procedure.
One more family declines surgery. The junior writes: "Without surgery the most frequent cause of death is brain abscess (68%), then stroke (17%), then hypoxic spells (13%)."
What is wrong?

choices.label: Hypoxic spells are the 68%, not brain abscess
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Link this back to the first case in this segment. Which event nearly killed that child tonight?
Tempting: stroke is dramatic and well known. But cerebrovascular accidents account for 17%, and brain abscesses for 13%.
The 68% belongs to hypoxic spells.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so fix the order in memory: hypoxic spells 68%, cerebrovascular accidents 17%, brain abscesses 13%.

say.text: Tempting: brain abscess sounds like the scarier complication. But the most frequent causes of mortality without surgery include **hypoxic spells (68%)**, with brain abscesses at 13%.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so fix the order in memory: hypoxic spells 68%, cerebrovascular accidents 17%, brain abscesses 13%.

say.text: Yes. Without surgery: hypoxic spells (68%), cerebrovascular accidents (17%), brain abscesses (13%).
Chronic hypoxaemia can cause hyperviscosity, abnormal haemostasis, stroke, **cerebral abscess** and endocarditis.
The junior's last line: "Once repaired, endocarditis is no longer a concern." Your verdict?

choices.label: Wrong, the risk remains repaired or not
Wrong, only repaired patients are at risk
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: The source names this risk for two groups of patients. Does the line leave one of them out?
Tempting: repair fixes the anatomy, so the infection risk seems fixed too. But patients with TOF, repaired or unrepaired, are at risk of **endocarditis**.
Tempting: you remember repair as the new risk. But unrepaired patients are at risk too; the source says repaired or unrepaired.
Yes. Patients with TOF, repaired or unrepaired, are at risk of **endocarditis**.
Back to the blue 9-month-old. Ten minutes in, still blue. A registrar says: "Give an IV vasodilator to unload the heart."
What do you say?

choices.label: Agree, vasodilate to ease the strain
No, raise resistance, for example with IV phenylephrine
Give furosemide first, it is heart failure

say.text: Tempting: unloading sounds kind to a strained heart. But this is a spell: knee-chest increases systemic vascular resistance, and phenylephrine increases systemic afterload.
Vasodilating moves resistance the wrong way.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is the reversed logic again. Every step raises systemic resistance or improves RV filling.

say.text: Tempting: a distressed blue child looks like heart failure. But spells need a rapid and aggressive approach, and the steps are knee-chest, oxygen, fluids, beta-blockers, phenylephrine and morphine as a sedative.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so remember: a diuretic is not on the list, and fluids are.

say.text: Yes. Raise systemic resistance: knee-chest increases it, and **IV phenylephrine** increases systemic afterload. Triggers like agitation, pain, anaemia, fever or hypovolaemia are what you prevent next time.
